title: Your Node.js Service Doesn’t Need a Rewrite. It Needs This
subtitle: Leverage native code speed with Node.js using ABI
excerpt: Leverage native code speed with Node.js using ABI
bodyHtml:
Your Node.js Service Doesn’t Need a Rewrite. It Needs This

Leverage native code speed with Node.js using ABI

Over the last few months I’ve had almost the exact same conversation with engineering teams. It always starts the same way “Our Node.js service is slow on this one endpoint. We’re thinking of rewriting the whole thing in Go.” Or “Our CTO wants us to move to Rust.”

And every single time, I’ve asked the same question back — “Is the whole service slow, or is it that one endpoint again?”

It’s always that one endpoint. The JSON parser on a 5MB payload. The image resize. The regex over a million-line log. The hash over a huge buffer. One hot path, pinning a CPU core, dragging the whole service’s p99 down with it. Meanwhile the other 90% of the code — the DB calls, the Redis hits, the queue publishes, is perfectly happy on Node.

If that story sounds familiar, this article is for you. Because the companies you are trying to emulate Vercel, Prisma, Parcel, Biome, 1Password — are not rewriting their stacks. They’re doing something much smarter and much quieter. They’re using Node.js native addons. Let me walk you through the whole thing.

Problem : rewrite tax nobody warns you about

A rewrite sounds heroic in a slide deck. In practice, it’s a tax nobody warns you about.

You burn three to six months of engineering time that could have shipped features. You walk away from the npm ecosystem — every internal SDK, every auth middleware, every observability wrapper you’ve carefully wired up. Your hiring pipeline, which is tuned for TypeScript, suddenly needs Go or Rust folks. And your Ops team now has to run two kinds of binaries, with two kinds of runbooks.

Here is the part nobody says out loud — in almost every Node microservice I’ve seen, 5 to 10% of the code does 90% of the CPU work. Rewriting the other 90% to fix the 10 is, honestly, a terrible trade.

Solution : escape hatch built into Node itself

Node ships with a built-in mechanism called Node-API (N-API) — a stable C ABI that lets any compiled language produce a .node binary which Node can require() like a regular npm package. Once loaded, it looks and feels exactly like a JS module. Your microservice doesn't know and doesn't care that the implementation underneath is native code.

And “any compiled language” is the important part. You can write a Node addon in:

  • C — the original, still works
  • C++ — historically the most common path via node-gyp
  • Rust — the modern favourite, via napi-rs or neon
  • Zig — growing ecosystem, especially for low-level systems work
  • Go — technically possible via cgo + N-API, but the runtime coupling makes it awkward (I'd personally skip this)

Node doesn’t care which language it is. It cares about the ABI. And N-API is ABI-stable across Node versions, which means you compile once and it keeps working across Node 18, 20, 22, 24 — no more node-gyp rebuild nightmares on every minor upgrade.

This is the key insight — the boundary between JS and native code is cheap. A Buffer passed across it is effectively a pointer. No serialization, no copy, no network hop.

Why this beats a separate microservice

I know what some of you are thinking — “Why not just run the fast code as a separate Go/Rust microservice and call it over gRPC?” It’s the second-best idea, and I see it all the time. But for a hot path, you pay for it on every single call:

  • Serialization — JSON or Protobuf, encoded on one side, decoded on the other
  • Syscall + network hop — yes, even over localhost
  • Context switch — two processes, two event loops
  • Ops overhead — another service to deploy, monitor, trace, and alert on

A native addon runs inside the same process. No sockets. No encode/decode. For a 1MB payload, you’re looking at microseconds of overhead instead of low-single-digit milliseconds. Multiply that by your RPS, and the bill at the end of the month tells its own story.

Picking the language

Historically, C and C++ owned this world. But almost every new Node addon I’ve seen in the last two years is written in Rust. There are good reasons:

  1. No segfaults taking your service down. In a C++ addon, one buffer overrun crashes the entire Node process. Rust refuses to compile unsafe code.
  2. No GC, deterministic latency. Rust frees memory predictably. Your p99 stops shivering.
  3. Cargo ecosystem. serde, tokio, rayon, regex, simd-json, image, zstd — a world-class set of crates, one line in Cargo.toml away.
  4. Real async bridging. napi-rs maps Rust tokio futures onto Node's event loop natively. No polling tricks, no libuv hacks.

And the proof is in who’s shipping it — SWC (Next.js, Vercel), Prisma query engine, the entire @node-rs/* family (bcrypt, argon2, xxhash, crc32), Biome, Turbopack, ast-grep, LavaMoat. Every one of these is a Rust addon embedded inside a Node process. You’ve probably been running several of them in production without realising it.

That said — if your team has deep C/C++ expertise, don’t throw it away. A well-written C++ addon is just as fast. The language choice is secondary. The pattern is what matters.

Code showdown

Following is snippet for performing hashing in Node.js

import crypto from 'node:crypto';
export const hash = (buf) =>
  crypto.createHash('sha256').update(buf).digest('hex');

Now the native addon via napi-rs:

// lib.rs
use napi::bindgen_prelude::Buffer;
use napi_derive::napi;
use sha2::{Digest, Sha256};

#[napi]
pub fn hash(buf: Buffer) -> String {
    let mut hasher = Sha256::new();
    hasher.update(&buf[..]);
    format!("{:x}", hasher.finalize())
}
# Cargo.toml
[lib]
crate-type = ["cdylib"]

[dependencies]
napi        = { version = "2", features = ["napi8"] }
napi-derive = "2"
sha2        = "0.10"

Build once with napi build --release. Import it from your service exactly like any npm module

import { hash } from './native';
app.post('/hash', (req, res) => res.send(hash(req.body)));

Your team opens the codebase and sees a regular import. They don't know and don't care that it's Rust underneath. That's the whole pitch.

For basic SHA-256 the gap is small, because both sides ultimately sit on hand-tuned C. The real delta shows up on workloads where pure JS simply cannot touch SIMD — JSON parsing, compression, image pipelines, regex over huge inputs. There, it’s routinely 5x to 20x.

Unblocking the event loop

Node’s event loop is single-threaded. CPU-heavy JS blocks every incoming request until it’s done. Native addons give you two clean escape hatches:

  • AsyncTask — offloads work to libuv's thread pool, returns a real JS Promise, keeps the event loop responsive.
  • An embedded runtime (tokio in Rust, std::thread in C++) — full native parallelism, completely independent of libuv.

This is exactly how the Prisma query engine serves hundreds of concurrent DB queries without clogging Node’s main thread. Your Fastify handler stays snappy while the addon chews through the actual work on dedicated cores.

  • SWC vs Babel : ~20x faster single-threaded, ~70x on four cores. Straight from SWC’s official benchmarks. Real-world Next.js build gains are closer to 3–5x once Webpack and other pipeline steps are factored in.
  • @node-rs/bcrypt vs bcryptjs : around 5x faster hashing, much lower tail latency under concurrency.
  • simd-json via addon : ~2–3 GB/s parse throughput on large, homogenous JSON payloads, against ~500 MB/s for V8’s JSON.parse. Real-world gains vary by payload shape.
  • Parcel 2 : scales linearly with cores because the addon uses Rust’s rayon, not the Node event loop.

These aren’t microbenchmark tricks. They’re the reason Next.js builds became bearable, and the reason Prisma can ship ORM ergonomics without ORM-level latency.

When to reach for an addon and when not to

Reach for a native addon when

  • An endpoint is genuinely CPU-bound — crypto, parsing, compression, image, regex, codec, ML preprocessing
  • You need deterministic latency (no GC jitter)
  • You need real parallelism without the memory cost of cluster

Skip it when

  • The bottleneck is I/O. Node is already excellent there, no addon will help.
  • The hot path is a few kilobytes of business logic. V8’s JIT will match native code for simple flows.
  • Your team has zero exposure to a systems language and the workload isn’t latency-critical. Don’t bolt on complexity you can’t maintain at 3AM.

The strategic cheat code

Here’s the part that really matters for Node-heavy companies. A rewrite is a political move. It forces hiring changes, stack changes, runbook changes. Everyone from the intern to the CTO has to buy in.

A native addon is a tactical move. The service stays a Node.js service. Same deploy. Same Prometheus scrape. Same OpenTelemetry trace. Same npm ci. One engineer writes the addon, publishes it to your internal npm registry as a prebuilt .node package, and every downstream team consumes it — without ever touching C, C++, or Rust.

That is exactly how Vercel ships SWC to every Next.js user on the planet. That’s how Prisma ships a Rust query engine to every Node backend running it. You get native-code performance without paying the organisational tax of a full rewrite.
